lessons.title: Working Capital Across Industries: FMCG, Retail, Capital Goods, Pharma and IT

children.text: A tile maker with a 90-day cycle is under strain. A jeweller with a 200-day cycle is running normally. An FMCG company with a cycle of minus 89 days is not lending money to anyone, it is borrowing from its suppliers by design. Judge any of them against the others and you will reach a confident, useless conclusion.

This lesson gives you the shape of the cycle in five industries, using FY2026 figures from the ratios section of screener.in, so that when you look at a company you know what normal looks like for its business model.
Eight Indian Companies, One Table

body.caption: Working capital profile, FY2026 (days, consolidated, from screener.in)

body.title: Cash conversion cycle vs working capital days, FY2026

children.text: Two things jump out. First, the spread is enormous: from minus 201 days to plus 228. Second, the two measures often disagree, sometimes violently. KEC International shows a cycle of minus 201 days but working capital days of plus 57. Hold that contradiction for a moment. It is the most instructive number in the table, and this lesson comes back to it.

body.text: Before comparing any two companies, ask whether they buy, make, store and sell in the same way. Sector labels are a shortcut for exactly that question. A business model decides the shape of the cycle far more than management skill does.

children.text: FMCG: The Suppliers Fund Everything

Hindustan Unilever turns stock in 61 days, collects from distributors in 19, and takes 169 days to pay its own suppliers. Nestle India holds more stock at 105 days, because milk and coffee procurement is seasonal and shelf lives are long, but still pays in 129 days and collects in 5.
Both end up with a negative
cash conversion cycle

. The reason is bargaining power. A supplier selling packaging or palm oil to a company of this scale accepts long terms because the volumes are large and the payment is certain. Meanwhile distributors pay almost on delivery, often against a bank guarantee or channel financing arrangement. Cash arrives before it leaves.

markDefs.definition: Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days. The number of days a business funds its own operations.

body.label: What a negative cycle buys you
body.context: When the cycle is negative, more sales generate more cash rather than consuming it. This is why large FMCG companies can expand distribution without raising working capital finance.

children.text: Retail: Two Opposite Worlds

columns.label: Avenue Supermarts (DMart)
points: Inventory days 37, because fast-moving groceries turn quickly
Debtor days 1, since shoppers pay at the till
Payable days only 8, as DMart pays vendors quickly to win better prices
Cycle around 29 days, funded easily from operations
The cash register is the working capital strategy

columns.label: Titan Company
points: Inventory days 222, because stores must display a wide range in gold
Debtor days 4, also a counter-sale business
Payable days 15, short terms from bullion and vendor suppliers
Cycle around 211 days, among the longest in Indian retail
The showcase is the working capital strategy

children.text: Same broad sector, opposite profiles. What separates them is the value density and turnover of what sits on the shelf. Note also that DMart's short payable days are a deliberate choice rather than weakness: paying vendors fast is part of how it negotiates the low purchase prices that fund its everyday low pricing.
Pharma: The Longest Legitimate Cycle

Sun Pharmaceutical reports 363 inventory days, 97 debtor days and 232 payable days, a cycle of about 228 days. Nothing is going wrong. Formulations pass through long validated manufacturing and quality release cycles, regulated markets require registered stock to be held in country, and distributors in export markets pay slowly.

Notice that working capital days sit at 54, far below the cycle of 228. The difference is everything outside the three trade lines: other payables, provisions, statutory dues and rebates. For a global pharma company, those are large.

body.title: Compute a pharma cycle
body.prompt: A generic formulations exporter reports inventories of ₹210 crore, trade receivables of ₹160 crore and trade payables of ₹120 crore, on sales of ₹600 crore and cost of goods sold of ₹300 crore. Using cost of goods sold for inventory and payable days, what is its cash conversion cycle, rounded to the nearest day?
body.explanation: Inventory days are 210 / 300 x 365 = 255.5. Debtor days are 160 / 600 x 365 = 97.3. Payable days are 120 / 300 x 365 = 146. The cycle is about 207 days, which is in the normal band for an export-facing formulations business and would be alarming for a grocery retailer.

children.text: IT Services: No Inventory, Only Collections

TCS has no meaningful inventory, so screener reports no inventory or payable days and its cycle is simply its debtor days: about 93. For a services business, working capital management reduces to one discipline, which is billing and collecting on time. There is no stock to trim and few suppliers to stretch.

The line to watch in an IT company is unbilled revenue, which is work delivered but not yet invoiced under the contract milestones. It sits in other financial assets rather than in trade receivables, so a company can show steady debtor days while the unbilled balance quietly grows. Read both lines together.

body.title: The services lever
body.textWithBlank: In an IT services business with no inventory, the cash conversion cycle reduces almost entirely to its ___ days.
body.explanation: With no stock to hold and few trade payables, collections are the only real working capital lever in a services business. TCS reported about 93 debtor days in FY2026.

children.text: Capital Goods and EPC: Where the Cycle Lies to You

Now back to the contradiction. KEC International, a transmission and infrastructure contractor, shows a cash conversion cycle of -201 days and working capital days of 57. Larsen & Toubro shows -151 and -27. On the cycle measure both look like they are funded entirely by others. In reality, project businesses are among the most working capital hungry in India.

body.title: Why a cycle of minus 201 days does not mean cash-rich

children.text: Payable days of 351 are not a sign that KEC pays its vendors after nearly a year. In project accounting, the payables line absorbs far more than ordinary supplier bills: subcontractor liabilities, accrued project costs not yet billed by vendors, and provisions for work executed. Divide that inflated balance by a cost of goods sold figure that excludes much of the project cost base and the resulting days figure balloons.
At the same time, project businesses carry two items the trade lines do not capture properly.
Retention money
is held back by the client for a year or more after the work is done.
Mobilisation advances
come in at the start and are adjusted against later bills, which flatters the position early in a contract and drains it later.

markDefs.definition: A percentage of each project bill that the customer holds back until the contract is completed and the defect liability period ends, often one to two years later.
An advance paid by a customer at the start of a contract, adjusted against later bills. It funds the contractor's early working capital.

children.text: This is why the broader measure of 57 working capital days is the more honest one here, and why EPC companies are always assessed on their net working capital as a percentage of revenue rather than on a cash conversion cycle. When you see the two measures pointing in opposite directions, trust the broader one and go read the notes.

body.text: Any time a screening tool shows a deeply negative cycle for a project, infrastructure or real estate company, treat it as a flag to investigate rather than a conclusion. Compare it with the working capital days figure and with the actual short-term borrowing on the balance sheet.

children.text: Putting the Patterns Together

stats.label: Suppliers fund the cycle
stats.context: Scale and certainty of payment buy long supplier terms, so growth self-funds

stats.label: Customers fund the cycle
stats.context: Counter collection offsets the stock, keeping the cycle short

stats.label: The balance sheet funds the cycle
stats.context: Long inventory is inherent to the product and must be financed

body.title: What drives the cycle in each industry

cards.definition: Long supplier credit against fast-moving stock and near-immediate distributor collection. Cycle is usually negative.
Counter sales collect in about a day, stock turns in weeks, supplier terms are short by choice. Short positive cycle.
Very high inventory days because gold and design range must sit in stores, offset only partly by counter collection.
Long manufacturing and quality release cycles, registered stock in export markets, slow-paying overseas distributors.
No inventory, so the cycle is essentially debtor days. Watch unbilled revenue alongside trade receivables.
Retention money, mobilisation advances and large project accruals distort the trade lines. Use working capital days instead.
Stock for production plus long credit to large original equipment buyers. Cycle is positive and often financed by bank limits.

children.text: One more way to feel the difference. Take two businesses each doing ₹500 crore of sales. At Titan's 211-day cycle, about ₹289 crore of cash is locked in operations. At HUL's -89-day cycle, operations release roughly ₹122 crore instead. Same revenue, a swing of about ₹411 crore in funding need.

body.title: Match the profile to the business
body.question: A company reports inventory days of 105, debtor days of 5 and payable days of 129. Which business is this most likely to be?
options: A civil construction contractor working on government projects
A packaged foods manufacturer selling through distributors
A software services exporter billing overseas clients
body.explanation: These are Nestle India's FY2026 figures. Near-zero debtor days point to distributor collections on delivery, high inventory days reflect seasonal agricultural procurement and long shelf lives, and long payable days reflect the bargaining power of a large buyer. A contractor would show high debtor days, an exporter would show no inventory, and a jeweller would show far higher inventory with short payables.

body.title: Benchmarking against the wrong peer
body.scenario: The founder of a specialty chemicals company with ₹300 crore of revenue reads that HUL runs a negative cash conversion cycle. Her own business holds 70 days of inventory, collects in 75 days and gets 45 days from suppliers, a cycle of 100 days. She tells her team to get the cycle to zero within two quarters, and instructs sales to demand advance payment from all customers.
body.prompt: Is the target reasonable? What would you tell her, and what would you target instead?
body.modelAnswer:
The target is not reasonable, and the instruction is dangerous.

HUL's negative cycle comes from its business model, not from effort: consumer goods that turn in weeks, thousands of small distributors who pay on delivery, and the scale to dictate terms to suppliers. A mid-sized specialty chemicals maker selling to a few industrial buyers has none of those levers. Demanding advance payment from customers who have alternative suppliers is the fastest way to lose them, and the cost of that lost revenue will dwarf any working capital saving.

What to benchmark against instead: two or three listed specialty chemicals companies of comparable size, using the same calculation method for each, over four or five years. That gives a realistic band.

What to target instead: a 10 to 15 day reduction in the cycle over a year, taken from the lines she actually controls. Cut finished goods inventory by improving demand planning, tighten collections on the slowest 20% of customers through a clear escalation process, and negotiate 60-day terms with the largest two or three suppliers at the next annual contract. On ₹300 crore of revenue, 15 days is about ₹12.3 crore of cash released, which is a genuine result. Chasing zero is not a plan, it is a slogan.

body.text: There is no universal right answer for the working capital cycle. There is only the right answer for your business model, and the only meaningful comparison is with companies that buy, make and sell the way you do.

body.label: Build your own industry benchmark
body.description: Open the Ratios section for three or four listed peers in the same industry, note debtor, inventory and payable days for the last five years, and you have a defensible benchmark band that no textbook figure can give you.

points: The cash conversion cycle across large Indian companies ranges from deeply negative to well over 200 days, and almost all of that spread is business model rather than management quality.
FMCG companies run negative cycles because scale buys long supplier credit while distributors pay almost immediately.
Grocery retail collects at the till and turns stock fast, while jewellery retail carries very high inventory, so the same sector label covers opposite profiles.
Pharma cycles are long by nature, driven by quality release timelines, registered export stock and slow overseas collections.
In IT services the cycle is essentially debtor days, and unbilled revenue must be read alongside trade receivables.
In capital goods and EPC, retention money, mobilisation advances and project accruals distort the trade lines, so the broader working capital days figure is more reliable.
Benchmark only against closely comparable companies, computed the same way, over several years.
